lesson.title: Same Object or Just Equal: is vs ==
lesson.summary: The == operator asks whether two values are equal in content, while the is operator asks the stricter question of whether two names refer to the literal same object in memory, and confusing the two is a common source of subtle bugs.
lesson.body:
You already know == from comparing numbers and strings, and you just saw how aliasing lets two different variable names refer to one shared list. Identity versus equality is the concept that ties those two ideas together precisely. == checks whether two values are equal, comparing contents; is checks whether two variables are references to the exact same object, comparing identity. For immutable values like small numbers, the difference rarely matters in practice, but for lists, and for mutable objects in general, it matters constantly.

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a

print(a == b)
print(a is b)
print(a is c)
```

This prints True, False, True. a and b are two separate list objects that happen to contain the same three numbers, so == says they are equal, but is says they are not the same object, because they live at different locations in memory; b was never made from a, it was built fresh. c, on the other hand, is a genuine alias of a, created with c = a exactly as you saw in the previous concept, so a is c is True: they are, quite literally, two names for one object. Python gives you a way to see this directly with the built-in id() function, which returns a unique integer identifying an object's identity; id(a) == id(c) would also print True, since is is essentially shorthand for comparing id() values.

There is a well-known gotcha involving is and integers that you should know about specifically so you avoid relying on it. CPython, the standard implementation of Python, caches and reuses small integer objects from -5 to 256 as an internal optimization, so x = 200 followed by y = 200 often makes x is y print True, even though you never made y an alias of x on purpose. This can make is look like it is safely comparing values for small numbers. It is not something the Python language guarantees, it is purely an implementation detail of CPython, and it becomes unreliable outside that cached range: typing x = 1000 and y = 1000 as two separate lines in an interactive session typically prints False for x is y, yet the exact same two lines written inside one function or script can sometimes print True instead, because the compiler is allowed to reuse identical constants within a single block of code. Because this behavior is inconsistent and implementation-specific, the rule to take away is simple and absolute: always use == to compare values, and reserve is only for the situations where identity is genuinely what you mean, such as checking if some_value is None, which is the idiomatic way to test for None in Python.
